The printed value is 3, while the alternatives come from counting all arguments including first, counting only the last argument and assuming rest parameters collect nothing.
questions.hint: Rest collects arguments left after the fixed parameters.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving functions — hoisting.
questions.explanation: Function declarations are hoisted with their bodies, so typeof reports 'function' even before the source line. Their value is available throughout the enclosing scope. The printed value is function, while the alternatives come from assuming declarations are not hoisted, expecting the return value instead and thinking the early reference throws.
questions.hint: Declarations, unlike expressions, are initialized during hoisting.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving functions — closures.
questions.explanation: The closure keeps n alive between calls; the first invocation raises it to 2195 and the second to 2196. Each call mutates the same captured binding. Carrying the operation through gives 2196; common slips include counting only the first increment and assuming the closure resets each call.
questions.hint: A closure retains the variable, it does not copy it per call.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving functions — call binding.

answer.exemplar: call explicitly sets this to obj, so get reads v and returns 2195. Without call, the detached function would not have obj as its receiver. The result is 2195.

questions.explanation: call explicitly sets this to obj, so get reads v and returns 2195. Without call, the detached function would not have obj as its receiver. A complete answer names 2195 and justifies it from the code rather than guessing.
questions.hint: call supplies the receiver explicitly at invocation time.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving functions — defaults.

options.misconception: Assuming a missing argument becomes zero
Thinking defaults do not apply to calls

questions.explanation: A default parameter is used when the argument is omitted, so label returns 2196. Passing undefined explicitly would also trigger the default. The printed value is 2196, while the alternatives come from assuming a missing argument becomes zero, thinking defaults do not apply to calls and adding one to the default.
questions.hint: Defaults apply when an argument is missing or undefined.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving coercion — loose equality.

options.misconception: Assuming different types are never loosely equal
Assuming the comparison has no boolean result

questions.explanation: Loose equality converts the string to a number before comparing, so 2197 and '2197' match and the result is true. Strict equality would keep the types distinct. The printed value is true, while the alternatives come from assuming different types are never loosely equal, guessing a coercion error and assuming the comparison has no boolean result.
questions.hint: The double equals operator performs type conversion first.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving coercion — truthiness.

options.misconception: Treating any positive number as false
Confusing the condition with a numeric result

questions.explanation: Any non-zero number is truthy, so a value of 2198 enters the first branch and 'yes' is logged. Only values such as zero and empty strings are falsy. The printed value is yes, while the alternatives come from treating any positive number as false, assuming the branch prints nothing and confusing the condition with a numeric result.
questions.hint: Remember which primitive values are falsy in a condition.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving types — typeof.

options.misconception: Thinking the variable was never set
Confusing a primitive with an object
Assuming the literal is quoted text

questions.explanation: typeof reports 'number' for numeric primitives such as 2199. Arrays and objects also report 'object', but a plain integer reports 'number'. The printed value is number, while the alternatives come from assuming the literal is quoted text, confusing a primitive with an object and thinking the variable was never set.
questions.hint: typeof returns a lowercase type name string.
